doc.title: Lou Marini interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 15, 2023

title: Why the phone rings, and the nature of ensemble playing
summary: Being pleasant, on time and a good listener; ensemble feel in Woody Herman's sax section, his father's sax arrangements, and Frank Wess on the Basie band breathing together.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: So I’m going to pose this question to you and I should tell you I asked Tom Malone basically the same one. And probably, like most successful musicians, you’re fairly modest. But can you tell me why your phone has always been ringing since basically when you started in the business? It’s a given that you’re a good player. But is there something else that young students should know about this path, where you arrived and how you got there?

Well it helps not to be a prick. You know the more prickly your personality is the better you better be as a player to maintain a successful career. Because you know Gadd and I talk about this a lot. One thing about all these guys that I’ve spent my life playing with, and still play with, is they’ve never lost the magic of music, the feeling of delight and the exploration and trying to get better. Everybody that I know that is in my cohort is still striving. And so if you’re on time, if you have a pleasant personality, and if you can play well, and if you actually listen to the other musicians, Walt and I were talking about this

yesterday. I’ve had experiences where, you know for me when I walk into a room and there’s other musicians playing I’m gravitating toward a center of pitch and an agreed upon place where we’re going to play, matching timbres, playing together. But there are some guys that you realize that they are by themselves. They are not listening to anybody else, and they don’t bend. So if you’re going to play with them you do the bending. But for instance like Alan Rubin, my colleague in the Blues Brothers Band and for so many sessions and stuff in New York, he played with you. Ronnie Cuber, our dearly departed, and another example of a prickly personality, but he played so great that you put up with it. But Ronnie could be a pain in the ass you know. But as far as like ensemble playing, when I was on Woody Herman’s band playing with Ronnie and Sal Nistico and Frank Vicari, man that was a delight. Because the written information on the page was like 2/3 of the information. The other third was all the subtle nuance that they had arrived at from playing together and that when you joined you had to pay attention and learn those things. But you could feel them coming to you. And that indefinable thing about ensemble playing is one of the — I don’t think Walt Fowler and I — we rarely discuss when to take a note off or how to attack a note. It’s just we arrive there and we do it in an unspoken way. And that’s the epitome of ensemble playing to me, and you know like playing lead alto or playing second alto or fourth tenor with good players in a well written saxophone part, that is so much fun. That’s something that never gets old you know. I have a bunch of arrangements of my dad’s for five saxophones. And they’re written so that they can be played just by themselves or with a rhythm section and then you can solo and play. And they’re just statements of the tune but when saxophone playing — when saxophone writing is really correct, and my dad’s was killer, man it’s just a delight to play that way. And then the more guys, the bigger the ensemble and the more together it is, Frank Wess told me that there were nights on the Basie band when everybody breathed together. He told me that they went to London one time and Basie said I don’t know why I’m paying all this money to ship the parts to London, you guys never look at the book anyway.
